occupants.value: An inferred household; no name is claimed
occupants.note: ADOPTED BY THE INFERRED-HOUSEHOLD PROGRAMME (docs/ROADMAP.md K1, phase two). This anonymous roof is the dwelling of an inferred laundress's household (2 of 3 this layer infers): hh_inf_laundress_north_02 in data/residents/households/. THE ROOF'S OWN EXISTENCE, POSITION AND FOOTPRINT REMAIN CONJECTURAL and are unchanged by the adoption; what the adoption adds is an argued occupant instead of an anonymous count-unit. The occupant is hypothesised from the town's demonstrable needs - the 1835 census of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings against the trades Andreas's 1833 roster names - and is not a person: no name is claimed and no figure is drawn.

residents.why: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. recon_1835_north_d2_029 is an anonymous inferred roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.
residents.basis: An anonymous roof of the reconstruction programme, ADOPTED by this household rather than raised for it. The roof's own existence and position stay conjectural; what the adoption adds is an argued occupant instead of an anonymous count-unit.

persons.name: A laundress (inferred resident, unnamed)
persons.note: HYPOTHESISED, AND NOT A PERSON. No source names this resident and none is claimed to: the record asserts that a town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings held at least this many households of this trade, and asserts nothing whatever about any individual. The name field carries a designation because inventing a surname would make this record indistinguishable at a glance from the documented layer beside it. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). THE SECOND OF 3 LAUNDRESS HOUSEHOLDS THIS LAYER INFERS. Andreas says the hotels and boarding houses of 1834 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides'. Four hotels, a garrison and the schedule's forty-two boarding houses generate washing in volume, and it was done by women. THE DOCUMENTED LAYER OF THIS DATASET HOLDS NOT ONE WOMAN IN A SERVICE TRADE - not because none were here, but because these sources name women almost exclusively as wives and as proprietors' widows. SEX IS STATED HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE IN THIS LAYER: the argument for the trade is explicitly an argument about women's work, so recording the person as male would contradict the reasoning that produced her.

residents.research_note: INFERRED HOUSEHOLD - second of 3 laundress households in this layer, in the north division. Andreas says the hotels and boarding houses of 1834 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides'. Four hotels, a garrison and the schedule's forty-two boarding houses generate washing in volume, and it was done by women. THE DOCUMENTED LAYER OF THIS DATASET HOLDS NOT ONE WOMAN IN A SERVICE TRADE - not because none were here, but because these sources name women almost exclusively as wives and as proprietors' widows. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one.
